factors.desc: Favorable or neutral coverage across the meta's IP archetypes and color strategies. With an expanded 15-deck meta field, decks with fewer polarized matchups perform more reliably across tournament swiss rounds.
Efficient AP usage and energy curve optimization for early and mid-game board development. Includes the ability to deploy threats ahead of curve and maintain proactive pressure.
Maximum damage output potential through Impact, Double Attack, Damage 2, and high BP thresholds. Measures how decisively a deck can close games once its win condition is assembled.
Overall value and composition of triggers in the deck's life area, including Color triggers for resource generation, Active triggers for board impact, and Final triggers for last-resort defense.
Reliable access to key characters and combo pieces through draw, search, and filtering effects. Decks that consistently assemble their core strategy outperform those reliant on natural draws.
Energy and AP economy, hand size management, and long-term card advantage. Measures how efficiently a deck converts its resources into board presence and damage over the course of a game.
Decision tree depth, AP sequencing complexity, and the gap between average and optimal play lines. Decks that reward mastery with significantly higher win rates score well here.
Ability to recover from life damage pressure, board wipes, and resource deficit through trigger activations, defensive keywords, and comeback mechanics.
Adaptable game plans, multi-color tech options, and the ability to pivot between aggressive and defensive postures depending on game state and matchup.

Ability to interfere with the opponent's board state, hand, or game plan through removal, Snipe, retire effects, and denial of key setups. Increasingly relevant as combo-oriented IPs populate the meta.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Eren Red midrange asks for regular Main Phase decisions about which Eren to deploy, when to commit Raid-driven spikes and when to use Hardened Punch to win a BP battle, but the plan is fairly linear and the cheap bodies carry much of the work. Sequencing matters around energy-line setup and when to Raid, though the order is mostly visible; errors cost tempo and life, and the deck's clogging risk is punished more than sharply lost.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Blue Ichigo Raid Midrange is a mid-tier competitive deck with several meaningful Main Phase decisions each turn, especially around AP budgeting between Raid and support costs and when to commit Rukia and Ichigo bodies. Sequencing matters somewhat (the 3 AP limit forces choices), but the deck is fairly straightforward and forgiving compared to highly interactive competitive shells. Its redundant Ichigo playsets make it fairly autopilot-friendly, so a new pilot can keep much of its win rate by making the obvious plays.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Ichigo Purple Raid Midrange asks the pilot to sequence Renji bodies into the energy line, chain Raids across the Ichigo versions, and time Bankai and Getsugatensho for a burst turn, giving more real decisions per turn than a straightforward aggro deck. Its strong mid-game Raid chains and Bankai ceiling let a good draw win on its own, but mistimed Raids, clunky hands from thin draw support, and early life pressure from aggro decks punish misplays moderately, placing it in the middle of the Standard field.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Purple Bomb Devil plays mostly on a curve of cheap Reze and Denji characters that reach the energy line in the Main Phase, so each turn has a fairly clear best play with some decisions about when to commit Bomb Devils and whether to spend Boom on a blocker. Its Raid payoff punishes poor sequencing of Denji and Reze but the deck is forgiving compared with more interactive or precise Union Arena decks. Its raw curve and strong Bomb Devil payoff win many games with competent but straightforward play, while matchup differences (faster decks versus outgrinding decks) make the plan shift somewhat.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Midrange Union Arena decks like this one make several meaningful choices most turns: when to deploy the cheap Himeno/Kon energy line, whether to hold AP for Raid setups, and which Aki version to commit. Timing matters less since most actions occur in the Main Phase, and the deck's main sequencing risk is version and energy-line management. Its mid-tier power and reliable curve let a straightforward pilot win a fair share of games, while the Raid conditions and slow start reward careful play in close matchups.

skillRating.label: Advanced
skillRating.reasoning: Yellow Eren/Zeke Raid is a midrange deck whose Raid timing, AP sequencing and choice between developing and pressuring give it frequent real decisions per turn. Its slow opening, dependence on matching Raid bases and thin hand repair make early misplays costly, while its power ceiling means a good draw still wins with obvious plays, so the autopilot factor is moderate.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Among competitive Union Arena Standard decks this is a relatively straightforward tempo list: a dense, cheap curve of Rei and Test Type-01 that makes the same smooth energy-line development most games, with a few real choices about when to commit the top-end threat and which targets to hit. Its near-absence of interaction means fewer lines to weigh, so decisions per turn sit mid-range and autopilot is high since the cards do much of the work.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other Standard Union Arena tournament decks, this tempo deck makes a moderate number of curve and attack decisions per turn, mostly straightforward once the energy line is built, with a few choices about holding Hot Bath or Rei/Mari bodies. Its cheap bodies and four-of playsets let the cards carry most of the win rate, so a pilot who plays the obvious curve keeps much of its strength, though close games are decided by attack sequencing and when to commit against blockers. Its low ceiling and lack of disruption make single misplays less dangerous than in higher-variance decks, but its weak finishing and matchup-dependent race against fast aggro keep the overall skill requirement near the middle of the field.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Blue Sukuna is a midrange deck whose turns involve real choices about energy colors, when to hold cards for Sukuna and Domain Expansion, and which Yuji or Nobara to deploy, placing it above simpler aggro lists. Its power ceiling and strong top-end finishers mean a good draw wins a fair share of games on its own, but close games depend on the pilot correctly surviving the early turns against fast decks and managing a diluted hand.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Compared with other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, this low-curve Purple Iori Samura aggro list asks for a handful of meaningful choices per turn: when to commit Iori Samura early, when to spend AP on Chihiro Rokuhira for the energy line, and when to hold Seichi Samura. Its sequencing is fairly direct, with limited response-window play, and a misplay costs tempo but is often recoverable given the deck's cheap bodies. Because the curve plays itself, a new pilot keeps much of the deck's win rate, though the thin draw and matchup-dependent race against faster Aggro-Tempo lists add some demand.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Yellow Cinderella Midrange is a fairly straightforward, mono-color midrange deck whose core Cinderella line appears in most openings, so the obvious play usually wins and the pilot faces a handful of meaningful choices per turn rather than long branching sequences. Its skill demand lies mainly in matchup-dependent pacing against fast tempo decks and in deciding when to commit bodies into high-BP or Snipe threats it cannot answer, while timing and sequencing requirements are modest. Errors are moderately punished because the deck is slow into aggression and lacks catch-up draw, but its redundant bodies recover from many small misplays.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Yellow Rem midrange-tempo plays a fairly straightforward curve of Rem and Ram that builds the energy line early, so most turns offer a clear obvious play with a few meaningful choices about when to spend AP on Raid plays. Sequencing matters mainly in the Main and Attack Phases, with moderate punishment for misordered turns given the narrow damage races, while the consistent cards keep the deck forgiving and let it win on its own when drawn well.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, Red Kenshin Himura Raid Midrange involves a steady stream of Raid-timing and energy-line decisions each turn, with moderate sequencing pressure around when to Raid onto an existing Kenshin and how to protect the base character. Its heavy 4-copy redundancy and Raid-driven curve make a competent draw play itself fairly well, which keeps the autopilot score high, while misplays around killing the base Kenshin or stalling on red energy are meaningfully punished.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Union Arena Standard tournament decks involve real turn-by-turn choices, so this aggro-tempo list sits mid-range: its curve of 1/2/3 AP cards and overlapping Heisuke/Taro/Shin names make most turns fairly direct, with Raid target selection and energy-line development as the main decisions. Its matchup spread is wide and punishes slow decks, so the pilot must recognize when to push and when a high-BP wall forces a different line, while its redundant core and forgiving curve mean the obvious plays win a lot of games on their own.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, Purple Shadow Army is a midrange deck with several meaningful Main Phase decisions per turn: sequencing the energy line with Purple requirements, choosing between deploying Shadow Soldiers and holding AP, and timing Raid chains. Its strong recursion and board presence let a competent but imperfect pilot still win, so its autopilot factor is moderately high, though misjudging early aggro pressure or Raid timing is punished.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, Green Kirito/Sinon is a straightforward aggro-tempo list: single-colour energy, heavy 4-of early characters and a clear curve, so most turns have one obvious play and the cards do much of the work. Decisions rise around when to commit characters and whether to hold Photon Sword or resources against blockers, and matchups matter because it folds to faster aggro and to Yuji or Heisuke, but its low resilience and weak triggers mean misplays are punished more than the easiest decks.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Blue Rimuru Raid Midrange asks for several meaningful choices per turn: which character to play to the energy line, when to Raid onto existing bodies, and when to spend AP on Feast or Report for card flow. Sequencing matters because Raid requires a valid base character already in play, and six Rimuru versions make hand construction and base availability a recurring read. Errors are moderately punished, since slow openings against fast decks like Heisuke or Yuji can lose a game and overinvesting in energy thins the front line, while the deck's large Rimuru top end still gives a forgiving fallback. Its power comes partly from strong top-end cards, so a new pilot keeps a reasonable share of its win rate.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Blue Roy Mustang midrange involves a recurring question of how to build the Blue energy line with cheap Riza bodies, when to deploy Roy and the Flame Alchemist board effects, and how to split resources between pressure and defense, giving moderate-to-high decision density for a standard competitive deck. Sequencing matters around energy-line setup and the BP battles, but errors are usually recoverable thanks to the consistent 3-4 copy staples, and its raw card quality lets a fair share of its win rate come from the cards themselves.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, this Zeke Jaeger midrange deck has a clear curve: deploy Pure Titans to reach the energy line, then play Zekes as the front line, so most turns have one obvious play with a handful of real choices about sequencing energy and when to commit. Timing matters mainly in the energy-line build and the mulligan-dependent opening, not in response windows, and its heavy Zeke density makes a strong draw play itself reasonably well. The main skill demand lies in managing clunky hands across six Zeke numbers and choosing between aggressive and defensive pacing against faster decks like Heisuke and Rem.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, Green Saitama is a straightforward midrange deck with a clear plan: build the energy line with King cards and deploy high-BP Saitama bodies, so most turns have one obvious play and sequencing rarely matters. Its skill demands come mainly from managing the energy line and knowing when the single Serious Punch and lack of draw leave copies stuck, plus adjusting its slow role against aggro decks. Overall it is moderately demanding but more autopilot-friendly than the most intricate decks in the format.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Hajime Saito Purple Aggro is a fairly straightforward curve deck: most turns offer an obvious play of Saito bodies and raid upgrades, so decisions per turn are moderate rather than heavy. Sequencing matters mostly in choosing when to raid and when to commit Gatotsu, and errors are recoverable within a field of cheap bodies, though a bad mulligan with no raid targets is hard to fix. The cards carry much of the win rate, so a new pilot keeps a good share of results, with the skill gap showing mainly in matchup-dependent attack timing against blockers.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Standard Union Arena, this midrange deck is mostly a straightforward curve-out-and-attack plan with a core threat (twelve Mereoleona copies) that is easy to find, so many turns have an obvious line. Decisions cluster around energy-line sequencing, AP spending, and when to commit removal, and the deck's tempo weakness against fast aggro means misjudged early turns can cost games. Overall it sits near the middle of competitive difficulty, leaning toward autopilot-friendly.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Attack on Titan Green Reiner is a midrange Raid deck whose turns involve real choices about which cheap bodies to deploy for the energy line, when to attack, and which Raid base to pair with which payoff. Sequencing matters because Raid must follow the correct base in the right Main Phase, and misjudging a turn-1 to turn-2 stumble or a duplicate-heavy hand can cost the game. Its power comes partly from the cards themselves, but converting a good draw into a Raid jump still requires skilled pilot decisions, so the deck sits above the simplest tier of competitive decks in Standard.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Hisoka-led Yellow midrange in Union Arena asks for steady per-turn choices about energy-line development, Raid timing and which front-line threat to commit, with a skill ceiling of 60 in the source data. Sequencing matters moderately around Raid and energy placement, and matchups shift between aggro and control, but full four-ofs and cheap energy bodies let the cards carry a good portion of the win rate.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, this Raid midrange deck sits above the simplest tournament decks: it asks the pilot to choose when to deploy Shin Asakura pairs, when to commit energy, and when to make Raid attacks, with several meaningful choices most turns. Its main line needs correct Shin-number pairing and sequencing, and a missed Raid chain or a wasted turn is hard to recover, but four-of redundancy and cheap early bodies let a competent draw win without expert micromanagement.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other Standard Union Arena midrange decks, this Mechamaru list asks for regular Main Phase choices about energy line and front-line deployment, plus a skill-dependent payoff from careful AP and energy sequencing. Timing matters less since its key plays happen in its own Main Phase, while matchups shift the plan against fast tempo decks. Its strong Aoi Todo depth and simple early energy line make it fairly forgiving on autopilot, though misplaying the AP ramp is costly.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Blue Levi is a midrange Union Arena deck whose core decisions revolve around which Levi variant to deploy, how to spend AP across the turn, and when to Raid onto a large-BP body, which gives it a moderate number of real choices per turn. Sequencing matters around Raid timing and energy-line setup, but the deck is less timing-dense than the most complex competitive lists, and its midrange plan is fairly stable across matchups while its power comes largely from straightforward Levi and battle-support cards. Errors (clunky draws, slow starts against aggro) are moderately punished, and the deck's power ceiling is middling, so a competent but not expert pilot can still convert a good draw.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Red Asta Aggro is a straightforward curve deck with consistent copy counts, so most turns have one obvious play and sequencing rarely matters beyond basic energy-line setup. Matchup adjustments matter somewhat against slower midrange and high-BP blocker decks, and errors like overextending or mistiming Demon-Slayer Sword can cost a race, but the list's simplicity keeps the pilot's ceiling moderate relative to other competitive Union Arena decks.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, this midrange green list asks for a steady stream of moderate decisions (what to deploy onto the energy line, when to commit Raid and Bankai) but little precise sequencing, since most turns play out in an obvious order. Its weak interaction and trigger suite mean misplays are moderately punished, mainly in races, while the strong Kenpachi packages and cheap bodies let the cards carry much of the win rate.

skillRating.label: Advanced
skillRating.reasoning: Makima control asks for a steady stream of choices each turn: which Makima variant to commit, when to hold removal-style effects, and how to spend AP and energy across a slow curve. Its power comes from disciplined sequencing against a field of faster decks, so a misplayed control turn is costly, while the redundant playset keeps the deck from being fragile to any single draw.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, Red Chainsaw Man is a fairly linear aggro-tempo list: a consistent four-of early curve of Denji, Pochita and The Power bodies gives mostly obvious turns, with some attack and blocking choices and occasional energy-line sequencing. Its narrow, redundant build means a good draw wins on its own, which keeps the autopilot score high, while its weakness to faster aggro and its reliance on drawing early plays give misplays and mulligan-level mistakes moderate punishment. Matchup variance is middling because the plan stays similar but the pilot must judge whether to race or hold blockers against faster versus slower opponents.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly

Sequencing matters around the Raid chain but there are few response windows to read, and with little removal or defensive recovery, errors mostly show up as lost races rather than harsh single-misplay collapses.

skillRating.label: Intermediate

Its thin disruption and limited draw mean a stumble in the first few turns is hard to recover from, while a stable board lets the obvious plays win a good share of games.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly

Sequencing matters mainly around energy-line setup and the Main Phase interaction timing rather than complex response windows. Matchup plans shift between racing aggro and grinding slower boards, and early mistakes can fall behind tempo decks, but the playset-heavy Envy and Lust bodies are forgiving and the deck's cards carry much of the win rate.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly

Its decisions center on raid and curve choices and when to commit, which is moderate for the format, while sequencing traps and misplay punishment are fairly light. skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly

Its low tempo and scarce draw make misdrawn hands and early life loss the main risk, while its high-BP front line lets a straightforward plan win many games without expert sequencing. skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, Yuna Midrange is a fairly straightforward deck: most turns center on building the energy line with cheap Yuna and supporting characters, then attacking with Asuna, so per-turn decisions are moderate rather than dense. Sequencing matters mainly in Main Phase AP and energy allocation and when to hold a character back, but there are few response-window traps since the deck plays almost entirely in its own turn. Matchup variance is notable because the deck is too slow against fast aggro and has little removal, so the right posture shifts considerably by opponent, and misreading that role costs games. Its cards carry much of the win rate on a good draw, but the close games are decided by the pilot.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Benimaru Raid midrange in Union Arena Standard is a mid-difficulty tempo deck: each turn involves real choices about AP allocation, which Benimaru version to deploy, and when to trigger Raid, but the curve is fairly linear and the energy line is single-color, so most turns have a clear line. Sequencing matters around Raid conditions and reserving energy-line characters, yet it is less order-sensitive than response-heavy decks, and misplays are usually recoverable against the middling Tier 3 field. The deck leans on its cards to win a fair share of games, though a competent pilot still has to win the damage race against faster aggro decks.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, Red Miroku is a midrange deck with a near-playset core and uniform openings, so most turns have fairly clear lines and the energy build is straightforward. Its skill demands come from balancing AP and energy development, deciding when to use Barrier, Wind Tunnel and Hiraikotsu during the opponent's attack, and choosing between even trades, which makes it moderately demanding without the sequencing or branching depth of the most complex decks. Its moderate matchup variance and limited tech mean misplays cost tempo more than the game outright, while a good draw that plays the obvious curve still wins a good share of games.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, this Red Chihiro Rokuhira midrange deck is a fairly straightforward plan: build the energy line with cheap bodies, then curve into Hakuri Sazanami and Kunishige. It asks for moderate per-turn decisions around AP and energy spending and some matchup awareness against fast aggro, but it has little draw, search or interaction to manage, so sequencing and timing stay simple. A competent pilot keeps most of the deck's win rate because the cards carry the plan, though close games turn on resource allocation.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Purple Shion midrange is a relatively straightforward deck built on four-of early bodies and consistent Rimuru and Diablo threats, so most turns have one obvious play and sequencing rarely decides games. Its skill demand sits mainly in managing the AP ramp and deciding when to commit energy-line characters, with moderate matchup adjustments against faster decks. Errors cost tempo but are usually recoverable, so the deck plays itself reasonably well in the hands of a new pilot compared with more intricate Standard archetypes.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, this Rurouni Kenshin Purple aggro-tempo deck is a mid-tier build with a fairly straightforward plan: build the energy line with cheap characters, then pressure with raids and attacks. Its decisions center on Raid timing and which attacks to commit into equal-BP blockers, which is more than a trivial deck but well below the most intricate lists. Its skill ceiling is moderate, and the deck wins a lot on the cards themselves when drawn well, though a slow opening hand is punished hard.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: As a Tier 2 aggro-tempo deck built on dense low-curve Yuji copies, the pilot's core job is sequencing the 1-AP and 2-AP turns and choosing when to commit pressure versus hold, which gives moderate per-turn decisions. Because the deck has little recovery and falls apart after a failed first wave, a misplayed attack or a mismatched race is punished fairly hard, while the sheer pressure of the curve carries much of the win rate on its own.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Purple Rimuru midrange asks for steady per-turn choices about energy-line development, AP spending and which raid target to commit, but its curve-based energy line and draw smoothing keep the average turn fairly direct. Sequencing matters mainly around getting the energy line and Rimuru online before the opponent's early pressure, and the deck's few removal options and slow start mean a bad allocation is costly, though its bodies and recovery keep mistakes from being fatal. Scored relative to other competitive Standard decks, it sits in the middle band with a moderate skill ceiling.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: As a midrange Union Arena deck with a consistent core of Edward and Alphonse copies, its turns offer a moderate number of real choices (what to deploy, when to attack, how to spend energy and AP) but the obvious line usually wins. Sequencing matters mainly around the energy line and when to commit the finisher, and the deck's redundancy means a single misplay is often recoverable. Matchup variance is meaningful because it must change its plan against fast Aggro-Tempo decks, while the consistent draws and cheap bodies let a new pilot keep much of the deck's win rate.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Within Standard Union Arena's competitive field, this Purple Naraku raid deck asks for real sequencing across the 1/2/3 AP ramp and careful raid-target selection, so it sits above a simple aggro list on decision density. Its raid line is fairly direct and it has modest card flow, so a competent pilot who follows the obvious raid chain keeps much of the deck's win rate, while misdirected raids and a sidelined target are costly and drive the mid-high error punishment.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, this Purple Sesshomaru midrange deck asks for several real choices each turn: which character to play onto the energy line, when to switch AP cards to rest, and when to Raid a sidelined body for a larger one, with positioning mattering in combat. Its slow curve and reliance on exact Sesshomaru number splits mean a misplayed sequence or a stalled hand can cost games, though the deck's raw Bakusaiga power and Raid replacements let a competent pilot win many games by playing the obvious lines.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, this Osaragi midrange deck is a straightforward character-based plan with several meaningful turn-by-turn choices around raids, energy line setup and when to commit characters, but few long sequencing traps. Its consistent multi-number Osaragi and Taro lineup means a competent pilot wins with the obvious plays, so autopilot is relatively high, while the lack of draw or removal makes mid-game resource and board decisions moderately punishing.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, this Green Nano Eiai Raid Midrange deck asks for several meaningful choices per turn: which Nano Eiai base to play, when to raid, and whether to commit to the front line or hold. Its raid stacks make overextending or exposing a stack to removal a real mistake, which lifts error punishment above average, while the sequencing demands stay moderate because the raid chain is fairly linear. Matchup variance is notable since it must race aggro decks such as Sakamoto Days and Re:ZERO while trading well with slow midrange. The deck's plan is fairly self-evident for a competent pilot, so autopilot factor sits near the middle.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to the other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, this midrange Tokyo Ghoul deck has a moderate number of turn-to-turn choices centred on energy-line setup, pacing against faster decks, and when to commit Kisho Arima. Its low-variance mono-red plan and consistent early curve let a pilot win many games by playing the obvious lines, while misjudging the tempo race or holding back the finisher is the main way to lose.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard's competitive field, this midrange Senjumaru Shutara deck has a steady curve with a moderate number of real decisions each turn, mainly about when to deploy characters and when to spend AP on the energy line. Sequencing matters around Bankai and the Royal Palace site, but the order of plays is rarely knife-edge. The deck's consistent core body and simple purple energy requirements let a new pilot reach a reasonable win rate, while its slow start and weak life triggers mean misreading the aggro matchups is costly.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, Red Kaneki/Ayato Raid Midrange sits in the middle of the competitive field: each turn asks which characters to deploy into the energy line, which to hold as Raid pairings, and whether to commit Raid attacks, but many turns have an obvious line. Sequencing matters in pairing Raid targets and paying AP before the energy line is set, yet the window is narrower than in control or combo-heavy decks. The high autopilot score reflects that a good draw of cheap Kaneki bodies, Naki and Half-Kakuja played in order wins a fair share of games, though misfiling copies across card numbers and losing tempo to faster decks still punish mistakes.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard's competitive field, this midrange Yellow Modernia deck sits in the middle: it has a clear energy-line build and a mid-game finishing pair, so most turns have an obvious line, but mid-game choices about spending energy and holding cards add real decisions. Its full playsets and lack of above-curve or answer cards make it fairly forgiving and autopilot-friendly, while its weak board interaction and matchup-dependent race against fast Yellow aggro keep the matchup and error scores moderate.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Rukia Freeze Midrange asks for a steady stream of decisions each turn: which characters to play to the energy line, when to build toward Raid steps, and when to use freeze and rest effects. Its reliance on specific base characters and Raid sequencing makes ordering matter, but the deck is not as intricate as the most demanding Union Arena builds. Its strong cheap bodies and freeze tools are fairly forgiving, while its need to assemble Raid chains and its weakness to fast tempo decks like Sakamoto Days make matchup reading and sequencing important.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard's competitive field, this red aggro deck makes a handful of meaningful choices per turn around energy-line development, Raid timing and when to commit Crossbow pressure, but most turns follow an obvious curve. Sequencing matters moderately (Raid and When Played ordering), and its lack of draw or filtering makes misplays in hand construction costly, yet the cards themselves carry much of its win rate.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, this midrange-control Natsuki Seba deck asks for a steady stream of Main Phase decisions around building the energy line, spending AP, and when to commit Seba copies, but most turns follow an established line. Sequencing matters mainly in getting the four-copy energy-line bodies and the correct Seba version online on schedule. Its plan shifts moderately between aggro and grindy matchups, and mistakes like a clunky hand or wasted support events are costly but usually recoverable, so the deck plays fairly straightforward once its main threat lands.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Karane Inda Aggro is a straightforward curve deck: cheap characters are deployed on schedule in the Main Phase and attacks are mostly obvious, so decision density and sequencing demands sit well below the typical competitive Union Arena deck. Matchup play adjusts somewhat (which threats to answer, when to commit versus hold blockers), and errors cost tempo but are usually recoverable given the redundant copies. The deck's power and consistency carry a large share of its results, so a new pilot keeps much of its win rate.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, this Uta-led Kaneki midrange deck asks for several meaningful decisions per turn around energy-line color and cost planning and Raid sequencing, placing it above the simplest decks but below the most intricate. Its skill ceiling is real: Raid timing and Step positioning reward careful pilots, and misplanned energy hands or wasted turns are noticeably punished against fast Aggro-Tempo decks. However, the four-copy Uta engine and consistent Kaneki threats let a straightforward line win a meaningful share of games, so the cards carry much of the win rate.

cardMetrics.desc: How many different decks or IP archetypes the card fits into, distinguishing cross-IP staples from IP-specific role-players.

cardMetrics.name: Power Impact
cardMetrics.desc: How much the card improves win rate when drawn or played, measuring its direct contribution to winning game states.

cardMetrics.name: Consistency Impact
cardMetrics.desc: How much the card contributes to reliable execution of the deck's core game plan through search, draw, or filtering.

cardMetrics.name: Meta Relevance
cardMetrics.desc: Current competitive usage rate and frequency across top tournament placements and winning decklists.

cardMetrics.name: Replaceability
cardMetrics.desc: How easily the card can be substituted without meaningful loss in deck quality; lower replaceability indicates higher importance.

cardMetrics.name: Synergy Value
cardMetrics.desc: How well the card enables or benefits from interactions with other cards in its archetype, measuring combo potential and IP-internal cohesion.
